summaries.example: Imagine you see a blue toy car. Moore would ask: are you aware of the blue car itself, or only of something happening inside your mind? He thought the blue you notice is not merely a private picture in your head. He also thought that ordinary facts, such as having two hands, are good starting points for thinking carefully.
summaries.summary: George Edward Moore was a British philosopher who helped make Cambridge an important center of analytic philosophy. He wanted philosophy to be clear and careful, and he often began with ordinary facts rather than with very large theories. Moore criticized idealism, the view that reality depends on minds or experience, and defended realism about many things in the world. He also wrote Principia Ethica, where he argued that goodness cannot be reduced to pleasure, desire, or another natural feature. In his work on perception, he considered sense-data: the colors, shapes, and sizes we directly notice. Later, his defense of common sense said that many everyday truths are known with certainty. Still, the source explains that his arguments left difficult questions about appearances, skepticism, and the deeper analysis of ordinary claims. Moore’s lasting importance comes less from one complete system than from the questions and arguments he gave to later philosophers.
key_ideas: G. E. Moore helped develop analytic philosophy at Cambridge with Bertrand Russell and Ludwig Wittgenstein.
He argued against idealism and defended a realistic view of ordinary objects and facts.
Moore said goodness cannot simply be defined as pleasure, desire, or another natural fact.
He studied how we see things and introduced the idea of sense-data, such as a color or shape directly noticed in experience.
His famous hand demonstration supported the ordinary claim that he had hands, but it did not settle every question about knowledge or reality.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moore shows that philosophy can begin with simple questions: What do we really see? What makes something good? Do we know that ordinary objects exist? His work teaches us to separate an everyday claim from a deeper question about what that claim means. It also shows that a philosopher can make a strong argument while still leaving important problems for later thinkers.

important_terms.definition: A philosopher who studies ideas by carefully examining ordinary words, claims, and arguments.
The view that reality depends in some important way on minds, thoughts, or experience.
The belief that many ordinary things and facts really exist independently of our thinking about them.
A basic fact or belief that seems obvious in everyday life, such as “the Earth existed before I was born.”
The value something has in itself, rather than value it gets from helping produce something else.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be real even when nobody is thinking about it?
Is something good because people want it, or could goodness be something different?
When an object looks different from how it really is, what exactly do we see?
Can an everyday fact be certain even if a philosopher raises doubts?

summaries.example: Suppose a straight stick partly under water looks bent. Moore’s early realism about experience cannot simply say that the stick itself is bent, because the appearance is misleading. His later sense-datum approach distinguishes the directly experienced visual item from the physical object, but then faces a problem: are sense-data physical parts of objects, effects produced by objects and our senses, or merely patterns in experience? Hallucination makes each option difficult, since there may be no physical object corresponding to what is experienced.
summaries.summary: G. E. Moore was a central British philosopher in the development of early analytic philosophy, although he resisted treating philosophy as a single program or as analysis alone. He first became known for attacking idealism. In “The Refutation of Idealism,” he maintained that an experience of blue should not be identified with a private mental content; awareness is directed toward something distinct from the act of awareness. His early metaphysics of propositions and truth later proved too simple, and his thinking changed as logical analysis made the status of false propositions clearer. In ethics, Principia Ethica argues that goodness is indefinable. Moore’s “open-question” reasoning challenges definitions that identify goodness with pleasure, desire, or other natural properties, though the source also discusses objections to this argument. He distinguishes intrinsic value from instrumental value and develops a controversial principle about the value of complex situations. His moral theory is consequentialist in structure but recommends established rules because outcomes are difficult to calculate. Moore’s work on perception introduces sense-data to explain misleading appearances, yet he never settles the relation between sense-data and physical objects. In common-sense epistemology, he treats ordinary truisms as certain while distinguishing their truth from their deeper analysis. His hand demonstration proves, at most, a simple empirical claim unless further metaphysical questions are answered. Moore’s enduring influence lies in his ability to expose philosophical phenomena, distinctions, and puzzles rather than in a finished system.
key_ideas: Moore’s rejection of British idealism rests on a firm distinction between a mental act and its object, though his early account of propositions and truth later changed.
In Principia Ethica, Moore argues that goodness is indefinable and that ethical questions cannot be reduced straightforwardly to empirical science or metaphysics.
His account distinguishes intrinsic value from instrumental value and from a contribution a thing makes as part of a larger situation.
Moore’s sense-datum theory tries to explain both ordinary perception and false appearances, but indirect realism, phenomenalism, and direct realism each create difficulties.
His defense of common sense asserts that ordinary truisms can be known with certainty while leaving open how those truisms should be philosophically analyzed.
Moore’s legacy is a set of arguments and problems, including Moore’s paradox: why is “It is not raining, but I believe it is raining” strange even if it could be true?
summaries.why_it_matters: Moore’s philosophy illustrates how apparently simple claims can support several different questions. “I have hands” concerns an ordinary fact; whether hands are independent of experience concerns metaphysical analysis; whether that fact can defeat skepticism concerns epistemology. Similar distinctions appear in ethics, where identifying a good outcome, defining goodness, and knowing moral truths are separate issues. Moore’s successes and unresolved problems helped shape later debates about realism, moral value, perception, certainty, and ordinary language.

important_terms.definition: The view that reality is fundamentally mind-dependent, or that ordinary objects are not fully independent of experience or thought.
The view that objects, facts, or truths are not made real merely by being thought about.
A philosophical method that clarifies a proposition by examining its components, logical form, or underlying subjects.
An experienced color, shape, size, or other primary object proposed by Moore to explain what perception directly presents.
The ethical view that goodness is not definable in natural terms such as pleasure, desire, or evolutionary advantage.
Moore’s term for the mistake of identifying goodness with some natural property or definition.
Value a thing has in itself, apart from its consequences or the context in which it occurs.
The position that moral rightness depends on producing the best consequences or outcome.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that goodness remains an open question show that it cannot be defined, or can definitions still be informative and revisable?
Can a proof that someone has hands establish the existence of an external world in a philosophically stronger sense?
If a sense-datum can occur during hallucination, what explains its apparent relation to a physical object in ordinary perception?
Should moral decisions be judged only by outcomes, or do relationships and personal responsibilities matter independently?
Why might a statement about one’s belief become absurd when combined with a statement denying what is believed?

summaries.example: You are looking at a white envelope under unusual lighting. It may look gray or yellow even though the envelope is white. Moore’s idea of a sense-datum says that you directly notice a patch with a certain color and shape, while the physical envelope may have different properties. But this raises a puzzle: is the noticed patch part of the envelope, caused by the envelope and your senses, or just a pattern in your experience? Hallucinations make the puzzle harder because someone may notice something that is not part of any physical object.
summaries.summary: George Edward Moore was a British philosopher associated with the Cambridge group that helped develop analytic philosophy. He preferred careful arguments to grand, all-encompassing systems. Early in his career, he rejected British idealism, which treated reality as closely dependent on mind or experience. Moore argued that thoughts and their objects should not be confused, and he defended a form of realism. His ethical book Principia Ethica made a famous claim: goodness cannot be defined simply as pleasure, desire, or another natural property. Moore called this error the naturalistic fallacy. He also distinguished intrinsic value, which something has in itself, from instrumental value, which depends on what it helps bring about. In his studies of perception, Moore introduced sense-data to account for the colors, shapes, and sizes we seem to notice directly. Yet false appearances and hallucinations made it difficult to explain exactly how sense-data relate to physical objects. Moore’s defense of common sense listed everyday truths and claimed that we know many of them for certain. His well-known demonstration of two hands was meant to establish the simple fact that he had hands, not automatically to end every skeptical argument. Moore’s legacy is therefore not one final theory. It is a collection of influential distinctions, arguments, puzzles, and challenges.
key_ideas: Moore challenged idealism and defended the thought that reality is not simply made by our minds.
He argued that goodness is not the same thing as pleasure, desire, or any other ordinary natural fact.
He separated intrinsic value from instrumental value: something can be useful without being valuable in itself.
His work on sense-data tried to explain why things can look different from how they are.
Moore defended common-sense beliefs, but he did not claim that everyday beliefs have only one possible philosophical analysis.
His arguments influenced later discussions of skepticism, perception, value, and the meaning of statements.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moore’s ideas help us notice that different philosophical questions can hide inside one ordinary sentence. A claim may be true in everyday life, yet still need analysis when we ask what its terms mean or what makes it certain. His work also connects everyday experience with difficult debates about perception, morality, and skepticism. Learning about Moore shows why philosophy often advances by making distinctions rather than by accepting the first explanation that sounds convincing.

important_terms.definition: The idea that reality is deeply dependent on minds, thoughts, or experience.
The view that many objects and facts exist independently of anyone’s thinking about them.
Careful examination of a claim to reveal its meaning, parts, and logical consequences.
A color, shape, size, or similar item that Moore proposed as something directly noticed in perception.
Moore’s claim that goodness cannot be defined as pleasure, desire, or another natural feature.
Value that belongs to something in itself, not merely because it leads to another result.
The view that the right action is the one that produces the best overall result.

questions_to_think_about: If a definition can still be questioned, does that prove it is not a real definition?
Does seeing your hands prove everything needed to show that an outside world exists?
What is the difference between an object and the way it appears?
Should the best results always decide what a person ought to do?
Why does it sound odd to say, “It is raining, but I believe it is not raining,” even if the speaker is mistaken?
